text:
B: Hi! Last one, yeah? I'm Hodan, Wembley.
A: Hello. Neil. Basingstoke. Yeah, I think this is the last one.
B: Thank God, my brain's going. How've you found it?
A: Fine, actually. Everyone's been very nice. It's more talking than I'd normally do in an evening, mind.
B: Ha! Not me, I could go all night. So what do you do? I had you down as a manager or a GP or something.
A: Er, no. Civil engineer. Water company. Pumping stations and sewers, north Hampshire. My wife's at a GP surgery, though, she's the practice manager. Part-time.
B: Oh, okay, so she knows the NHS chaos. I'm a pharmacy technician, senior, at a hospital in North West London. Aseptic and dispensary.
A: She'd get on with you, I think. She's always on about prescriptions going missing between the surgery and the chemist.
B: Honestly, that's half my life. Somebody upstream doesn't do their job properly and then it lands on us and we look like the problem. I keep a spreadsheet of every near-miss in the department, so when anyone tries it, I've got it in black and white.
A: That's sensible. I'm the same with the pump stations. If you've written it down, nobody can argue with you.
B: Exactly! See, people think it's petty but it's not.
A: No.
B: What do you do outside work, then? You seem like a garden person.
A: Yeah, a bit. Tomatoes, runner beans. Walk the dog. Watch Reading lose.
B: Reading! Oh, that's rough. I'm Arsenal, well, my brothers are, I just watch with them for the arguing.
A: Arsenal's a bit of a different experience, I'd imagine.
B: Ha, yeah, we complain when we draw. Did you have a bad commute today? The Jubilee line was down again, I was stood on a platform for twenty minutes and then I got a parking ticket last week, which I'm appealing, by the way, on principle, because the sign was literally behind a tree.
A: Behind a tree?
B: Behind a tree! I've got photos.
A: You'll win that, then. Er, mine's the A33. Roadworks. Nothing exciting.
B: Do you have kids? Sorry, I always ask everyone that.
A: That's all right. Two, both grown up. Daughter's in Southampton, son's at Nottingham. Your lad's eight, isn't he? I saw the photo.
B: Yeah, Idris. He's at the age where he asks a question every five seconds. My mum does his pickups when I'm on lates, I don't know what I'd do without her. She's getting older, though, and I kind of rely on her a lot. Anyway.
A: Yeah. Mine's seventy-nine, on her own in Reading. You don't really notice it happening, and then you do.
B: Yeah. That's it, you know.
A: Make the most of her, I suppose. That's about all you can do.
B: Erm, yeah. Fair. Sorry, that got deep for a last call.
A: No, that's fine. Better than the weather.
B: Ha! Okay, quick one, Cornwall or abroad?
A: Cornwall. Padstow. Every year.
B: Every year? You don't get bored?
A: No. That's sort of the point.
